messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Luis Alvarez was 55 when he first came to treatment, a divorced fashion designer who had spent most of his adult life trying to build a polished, controlled world around himself. He described growing up in North America in a home where his caregiver, his father, struck him regularly and unpredictably. He did not give a single tidy account of the abuse; even as an adult, he could not tell the story in a clear sequence. When he tried, he would pause, lose his place, and say that the memories came back in fragments rather than as something he could line up from beginning to end. What he could recall often felt oddly distant, as if it had happened to someone else. He would describe one scene or another — a hand coming down, the sharp humiliation of being cornered, the sense of his body bracing before impact — and then abruptly notice that he felt numb, almost blank, despite knowing the memories were his own. Each time he returned to these recollections, the feeling that came with them was not only fear but intense guilt, as if he should have done something different, said something different, or somehow prevented what happened.

As an adult, Luis built a career in fashion partly because it let him work in a realm of surfaces, lines, and presentation, where he could control how things appeared. Yet the old sense of danger never fully left him. He was on guard even inside his own home, checking door locks twice and keeping background noise on in the evenings because silence could feel menacing to him. An unusually quiet apartment, especially after he had come home from work and the bustle of the day had fallen away, could bring on a sharp sense that something bad was about to happen. He did not describe this as a vague unease but as a bodily readiness, as if he had to listen for the next blow. He also startled badly when touched without warning. In the studio, if an assistant tapped his shoulder from behind to ask a question, he might jolt and turn too quickly, embarrassed by how instantly alarmed he became. Even affectionate gestures could catch him off guard if he had not seen them coming, and he experienced his own reaction as excessive and hard to explain.

Over the years he had also become preoccupied with what had been done to him and with what he believed he had done wrong in response. He would dwell on the cruelty of the abuse, turning over scenes of his father’s behavior and the injustice of it, but he would also ruminate on his own childhood reactions, wondering why he had not been tougher, quieter, or more capable of stopping it. These thoughts did not settle into a coherent narrative; instead, they looped. At night, he would sometimes wake from dreams that he dreaded because they often followed the same emotional shape, leaving him unsettled for hours afterward. He had learned to avoid the times of day that tended to bring those nightmares on, especially late evening, when his mind could wander and the house became still. He would stay busy at work far into the night or keep the television on at home to push back against the quiet. When he could not avoid it, he felt himself returning to the same internal arguments about others’ cruelty and his own supposed failings.

Luis came to believe that the abuse had permanently changed him for the worse. He spoke of himself as someone who could never fully relax, trust, or feel safe in the ordinary way other people seemed to. That mistrust colored his relationships after his divorce, leaving him wary of relying on anyone for long. He said he knew, intellectually, that not everyone would hurt him, but emotionally he could not shake the sense that people could not be trusted. What frightened him most lately was the thought that the intensity of his reactions meant he was going crazy. He did not describe hallucinations or loss of reality testing; rather, he was alarmed by how abruptly his body and mind seemed to respond to ordinary events, especially silence or unexpected touch, and by how impossible it felt to make his memories line up into something coherent. By the time he sought help, he was tired of living as though danger might enter his home at any moment, tired of the nighttime dread, and tired of the shame that followed every attempt to remember. He hoped treatment might help him understand what had happened without being flooded by guilt or fear, and he wanted to know whether he could ever feel safe in his own life again.
